summary_html: A **court reverses or vacates** a CPS or agency decision due to procedural error, insufficient evidence, or constitutional violation. Federal review data (CFSR, ASFA) tracks judicial determinations on reasonable efforts and due process.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — judicial findings of 'reasonable efforts' compliance  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of judicial/agency conformity  
- **42 U.S.C. § 1983** — civil-rights remedy for unconstitutional removals (14th & 4th Amendments).

key_cases.holding: Where the juvenile court waited twenty months after the evidentiary hearing to enter a written termination order, it abused its discretion by refusing the mother's motion to reopen the record with contemporary evidence of sobriety, housing, and employment; the termination order was reversed and remanded.
key_cases.relevance: A leading Iowa Supreme Court reversal of a juvenile court order for procedural error — inordinate delay plus refusal to reopen the record.
key_cases.quote: We reiterate for emphasis that DHS's reasonable efforts obligation continues until either a final written termination order or a waiver by the juvenile court

key_cases.case_name: Iowa Department of Health and Human Services v. Iowa District Court for Polk County
key_cases.holding: A juvenile court acts within its authority under Iowa Code section 232.102(1)(b)(1) when, at an interested party's request, it temporarily stays HHS from moving a child in its custody until it can hold an evidentiary hearing; review of an HHS placement decision may be prospective as well as retrospective.
key_cases.relevance: Reverses an appellate ruling that had stripped the juvenile court of prospective review, restoring judicial power to check agency placement decisions.
key_cases.quote: The juvenile court "shall give deference" to HHS's placement decision, but deference does not mean blind acceptance that freezes the juvenile court out of any meaningful review of HHS's decision.

key_cases.case_name: Grant v. Iowa Department of Human Services
key_cases.holding: Issue preclusion may not be used to dismiss an application under Iowa Code section 235A.19 to correct a founded child-abuse assessment merely because a district court in a parallel visitation proceeding already resolved the same predicate fact; the district court judgment was reversed and the case remanded to DHS for a hearing on the correction request.
key_cases.relevance: A reversal of an agency dismissal for an erroneous interpretation of law under Iowa Code section 17A.19(10)(c), and a concrete example of the judicial check on a DHS refusal to revisit its own child-abuse determination.
key_cases.quote: the legislative policies and goals are best served by allowing the DHS to correct its own assessment of a child abuse report free from the doctrine of issue preclusion
